title: Studio 90 · AI, football and the new jobs

slides.name: 1 · Teacher page

params.text:
Students map how AI and new technology have remade football, place the new jobs on one line from the pitch to the call, argue about authorship and data, then design a football job for 2035.
About 60 minutes. It runs like a studio: sheets, a wall chart, an atlas, a crit and a brief.
No phones needed. Votes are hands up; the brief is pen and A3, or one slide per team.

slides.notes:
RUNNING ORDER · ABOUT 60 MINUTES
· 00 Open studio — 6 min: cover, the claim, the session as a studio, which job is real?
· 01 The game, remade — 12 min: the wall chart, six moments, old game and modern game, pair talk
· 02 Under the hood — 7 min: the line, three things AI does, the numbers
· 03 The job atlas — 17 min: the atlas, five studios (cover and jobs each), how new is this job?, hybrid skills
· 04 The crit — 7 min: who is the author?, AI and people, myth or fact, whose data?
· 05 The brief — 11 min: the brief, the poster, the crit rules, pin-up

FOR 45 MINUTES. Hide "Old game, modern game", the numbers, "How new is this job?" and myth or fact, and give the brief 8 minutes.

THE BIG IDEA. Football is now a production: the match is captured, engineered, modelled and designed before a person makes the call. Every one of those steps is somebody’s job, and many of them are design jobs. The line (sheet 02) is the spine: the atlas, the crit and the brief all hang off it.

THE MOVE THAT MAKES IT WORK. Do not sell the technology. Every studio has a catch, and the crit is where the room argues with it.

SOURCES (also in each slide’s notes). Premier League, “Semi-automated offside technology: what you need to know” (April 2025). Adidas, the Al Rihla connected ball release (2022). CBS Sports and FIFA on referee body cameras at the Club World Cup (June 2025); IFAB on body-camera trials. Ingenia and Buro Happold on Tottenham Hotspur Stadium’s dividing pitch; The Stadium Business and ENR on the Bernabéu’s 360° screen (Daktronics). BusinessCloud (2018) on Southampton’s virtual boards (ADI and Supponor). Training Ground Guru and These Football Times on Thomas Grønnemark; Brentford FC (May 2024) on Bernardo Cueva. Leeds United’s data engineer/scientist advert (UK Sport jobs, June 2025). Business Today (24 July 2026) on Arsenal’s research engineer. BBC Sport (6 March 2026) on Reading’s head of AI. The Mirror (2022) quoting Liverpoolfc.com on William Spearman. Liverpool.com (January 2020) on the 1.3% goal probability. Google DeepMind, TacticAI (Nature Communications, March 2024). The Analyst on set-piece goals in 2025–26. BCAM on the San Mamés digital twin. World Economic Forum, The Future of Jobs Report 2025.

CHECK BEFORE YOU TEACH. Job adverts move fast: the Leeds and Arsenal adverts are cited as reported, and may have closed. Swap in a current advert from Jobs In Football or Training Ground Guru if you have one.

slides.name: 2 · Framed picture
slides.notes: COVER · up as they come in. Ask the door: "Name a job at a football club that is not player, manager or referee." Keep a list on the board; come back to it at the atlas.

slides.name: 3 · Statement · frame

params.text: In 2018 a club hired a man to teach its players how to throw the ball in.
Liverpool FC · the weirdest job in football

slides.notes:
OPEN · 1 MINUTE. Thomas Grønnemark, a Danish throw-in specialist, was hired by Jürgen Klopp in July 2018, reportedly the Premier League’s first dedicated throw-in coach. He called it “the weirdest job in football”. Liverpool had been 18th of 20 for keeping the ball from a throw-in under pressure in 2017–18.

Sources: These Football Times (March 2020), Training Ground Guru, Liverpoolfc.com.

Ask: "Weird, or just new? What makes a job look weird?" The answer we want by the end: it looks weird because nobody had measured throw-ins before. Data makes new jobs.

slides.name: 4 · Today runs like a studio

params.text: A wall chart of how football changed, and six moments up close.
One line from the pitch to the call, and what AI does on it.
Five studios, twenty-five jobs, and where you fit.
We argue about authorship and data, then your team designs a football job for 2035.

slides.notes:
OPEN · 1 MINUTE. Frame the hour as a studio session, not a lecture: we build a wall, then crit it. The output is theirs: a job poster per team.

If the room is a design course, say it plainly: half the jobs on the atlas are design jobs.

slides.name: 5 · Which of these is a real football job?

params.text: Which of these is a real football job?
Teaches players to use a throw-in as an attack.
Turns set pieces into a science.
Builds AI tools for the first-team analysts.
Runs AI across recruitment, tactics and the business.

slides.notes:
OPEN · 2 MINUTES. Read each card, hands up if they think it is real. Then the next slide: all four are.

Throw-in coach: Thomas Grønnemark, Liverpool, 2018. Tactical statistician: Bernardo Cueva’s title at Brentford, where he ran set pieces, before he left for Chelsea in 2024 (Brentford FC, May 2024). Research engineer: Arsenal advertised one for its men’s first-team analysis in July 2026 (Business Today, 24 July 2026). Head of AI: Reading appointed Stuart Fenton, reported as the first at an English club (BBC Sport, 6 March 2026).

slides.name: 6 · Statement · frame

params.text: All four are real. None of them was a job in 2010.

slides.notes: OPEN · 30 SECONDS. Let it land. Then: "So how did football get here? Sheet one."

slides.name: 7 · Framed picture
slides.notes: PART 01 · 12 MINUTES. The wall chart, then six moments up close: the ball, the line, the referee, the pitch, the boards, the screen.

slides.name: 8 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
PART 01 · 2 MINUTES. THE WALL CHART. Walk it left to right, one sentence each. The pattern to point at: the early changes help the referee; the later ones are about the club, the broadcast and the fan. And the last stop is people: the newest change is the job titles.

2013: Hawk-Eye goal-line technology in the Premier League from 2013–14. 2015: FIFA’s law change allowing electronic performance and tracking systems (GPS vests) in matches. 2018: Grønnemark at Liverpool; Southampton’s virtual hybrid boards (BusinessCloud, 2018). 2019: VAR in the Premier League from 2019–20; Tottenham Hotspur Stadium opened in April 2019. 2022: Adidas Al Rihla with a 500 Hz sensor, and FIFA’s semi-automated offside at Qatar 2022. 2024: TacticAI, Google DeepMind with Liverpool (Nature Communications, March 2024). 2025: semi-automated offside in the Premier League from 12 April 2025; referee body cameras at the FIFA Club World Cup, June 2025. 2026: Reading’s head of AI (BBC Sport, March 2026); Arsenal’s research engineer advert (Business Today, July 2026).

Ask: "What is missing from this chart?" (Good answers: the women’s game, fans’ phones, betting, video games like EA FC that taught a generation to read stats.)

args.caption: The game, remade · the wall chart

slides.name: 9 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
MOMENT 1 · 1 MINUTE. Adidas’s Al Rihla, the 2022 World Cup ball, held a 500 Hz inertial measurement unit (a motion sensor) suspended at its centre. It reported every touch to the video match officials within seconds, and with player tracking it fed FIFA’s semi-automated offside. Built with FIFA and KINEXON. The balls had to be charged before a match.

Source: Adidas news release, “adidas reveals the first FIFA World Cup official match ball featuring connected ball technology” (2022). The “no change in performance” claim is Adidas’s.

Ask: "If the ball is a device, who designs it: a kit designer or an electronics engineer?" (Both. That is the point.)

args.caption: Moment 1 · The ball is a sensor

slides.name: 10 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
MOMENT 2 · 2 MINUTES. Semi-automated offside technology began in the Premier League on 12 April 2025, after the FA Cup. Up to 30 cameras in each ground, several at 100 frames a second, twice broadcast rate, track the players’ bodies. The system suggests the kick point and draws the lines; the VAR checks and approves; then a 3D decision visual of the players, in their kits, goes to the big screen and to TV. Built with PGMOL and Genius Sports. The league says it makes decisions faster and more consistent, not more accurate.

Source: Premier League, “Semi-automated offside technology: what you need to know” (April 2025).

THE DESIGN POINT. Somebody designed those 3D players: their proportions, the camera angle, the red and green lines, how long the replay holds. That picture is the decision fans see. Ask: "Is that a referee’s job or a designer’s?"

args.caption: Moment 2 · The offside line is a render

slides.name: 11 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
MOMENT 3 · 1 MINUTE. At the FIFA Club World Cup in the USA (June–July 2025), referees wore a small camera on their headset. The footage went into broadcasts after a check, mainly for non-controversial moments, and into referee training. Pierluigi Collina said it went “beyond our expectations”. The IFAB then opened body-camera trials to competitions worldwide, but FIFA does not pay for them.

Sources: CBS Sports (June 2025); Soccerway and AFP reporting Collina; IFAB trials page.

Ask: "Who chooses which referee clip you see? That is an editor’s job."

args.caption: Moment 3 · The referee is a camera

slides.name: 12 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
MOMENT 4 · 1 MINUTE. Tottenham Hotspur Stadium (opened 2019, designed by Populous) has the world’s first dividing retractable pitch: the grass splits into three trays and rolls under the South Stand, revealing an NFL artificial pitch below. It was the feature that won the club its NFL deal. The touchline and tunnel ramps rise and fall to meet either surface.

Sources: Ingenia, “Tottenham Hotspur Stadium: the football pitch in three pieces”; Buro Happold; Dezeen.

The point: a stadium is now a venue that is football one night and a concert or NFL game the next. That makes jobs: venue producers, event designers, turf scientists.

slides.name: 13 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
MOMENT 5 · 1 MINUTE. Virtual advertising: fans in the ground see one advert on the pitch-side boards, and TV viewers in each country see a different one, laid over the picture so players still run in front of it. Southampton installed ADI and Supponor’s “Virtual Hybrid” boards in 2018; the Bundesliga and LaLiga have used it for international broadcasts. One board, sold many times.

Sources: BusinessCloud, “Southampton FC signs revolutionary advertising deal” (2018); Inside World Football on the Bundesliga.

Ask: "If every country sees a different match, what is the real match?"

args.caption: Moment 5 · The board you see isn’t the board they see

slides.name: 14 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
MOMENT 6 · 1 MINUTE. The rebuilt Santiago Bernabéu in Madrid has a 360° video scoreboard hanging from the roof: 18 LED screens, part of over 3,700 square metres of LED supplied by Daktronics, and a retractable roof and pitch for concerts. ENR named it a 2025 Global Best Project.

Sources: The Stadium Business (April 2022) on the Daktronics deal; ENR, 2025 Global Best Projects.

The design point: 3,700 square metres of screen needs content every second of a matchday. Somebody designs it: motion designers, live graphics operators, creative directors. That is a studio inside a stadium.

args.caption: Moment 6 · The roof is a screen

slides.name: 15 · The old game and the modern game

params.text: The old game and the modern game
A sensor reporting 500 times a second.
Thirty cameras, a skeleton and a 3D replay.
Grass that rolls away for the NFL.
A different advert in every country.
Specialists for throw-ins, set pieces and the mind.

slides.notes: PART 01 · 2 MINUTES. One row per click. On each, ask: "Who has a new job because of this change?" Write the answers on the board under the cover list: tracking operator, ball electronics, broadcast designer, POV producer, venue producer, virtual ad producer, specialist coach.

slides.name: 16 · Statement · frame

params.text: Which change made football better to watch? Which made it worse?

slides.notes:
PART 01 · 2 MINUTES. Pairs pick one of each from the six moments. Take three pairs.

Push them: "Better for whom: the fan in the ground, the fan on TV abroad, the player, the club’s finance director?" The same change can be all four.

slides.name: 17 · Framed picture
slides.notes: PART 02 · 7 MINUTES. The line every job sits on, what AI does on it, and three numbers.

slides.name: 18 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
PART 02 · 2 MINUTES. THE SPINE OF THE SESSION. Take one example along the whole line: an offside. Capture: thirty cameras track every player’s joints. Engineer: the frames are synced with the ball’s touch data. Model: computer vision finds the bodies and the kick point. Design: a 3D picture of the decision. Decide: the VAR approves it, and the referee gives it.

Then ask: "Where does the designer sit, and why is it before the decision, not after?" Because the picture shapes how the call is seen and checked.

This is a simplification: real clubs loop back (a coach’s question changes what is captured next).

args.caption: From the pitch to the call

slides.name: 19 · Three things AI does in football

params.text: Three things AI does in football
Computer vision finds players, joints and the ball in video. The offside skeleton, the highlight clipper.
Machine learning and simulation turn past matches into chances: an injury risk, a goal probability, a season played 10,000 times.
Generative AI writes, draws and talks: match reports, fan chatbots, kit concepts, a highlight voiced in your language.

slides.notes:
PART 02 · 2 MINUTES. Short for a university room; they will know the terms. Make one link per card to the line: seeing is capture into model; predicting is model; making is design.

TacticAI (Google DeepMind with Liverpool, Nature Communications, March 2024) predicted corner-kick outcomes and suggested player positions; Liverpool’s experts preferred its suggestions to existing tactics about 90% of the time in the study. Name it as the study’s finding.

Ask: "Which of the three would a design studio use most?" (Make, then see.)

slides.name: 20 · The numbers behind the modern game

params.text: The numbers behind the modern game
Chance of a goal in the next 15 seconds — Liverpool’s model, from where the ball and players are
Premier League goals from set pieces, 2025–26 — not counting penalties: the second-highest share in 34 seasons
Liverpool’s league goals from throw-in situations, 2019–20 — the season after the throw-in coach arrived

params.label: Takeaway
params.text: Sources: Liverpool.com (January 2020) · The Analyst (Opta) · Training Ground Guru

slides.notes:
PART 02 · 2 MINUTES. Three numbers, one argument: measuring a part of the game makes a job for it.

1.3%: Liverpool’s data scientist Tim Waskett showed at the Royal Institution Christmas Lectures how every moment becomes a goal probability (Liverpool.com, January 2020). 27.4%: The Analyst’s figure for non-penalty set-piece goals in the 2025–26 Premier League, the second-highest in the competition’s history. That is why clubs hire set-piece coaches. 14 of 85: the figure most often cited for Grønnemark’s impact; do not credit it all to him.

Ask: "Which part of the game has nobody measured yet?" (Good answers: communication between players, the crowd’s effect, a goalkeeper’s voice.) That is a job waiting to exist; hold it for the brief.

slides.name: 21 · Framed picture
slides.notes: PART 03 · 17 MINUTES. The heart of the session. The atlas, then each studio: its cover, its jobs and a real case.

slides.name: 22 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
PART 03 · 2 MINUTES. THE ATLAS. Five studios, one per step on the line. Twenty-five jobs; some are long-standing but changed by AI (sports scientist, data protection officer), some are new (research engineer, head of AI, virtual ad producer).

Tick off the cover list from the start: which jobs did the room already name, and which are new to them?

Say what the atlas is: our grouping, built from real adverts and reports, not an official list. Studios overlap; a data visualisation designer sits between Model and Design.

slides.name: 23 · Framed picture
slides.notes: STUDIO A · 30 SECONDS. Capture: the people who turn a match into data.

slides.name: 24 · Studio A · Capture

params.text: Runs the camera rigs that track every player, 25 to 100 times a second, for offside and for the analysts.
Reads GPS vests and heart rates to manage training load. An old job, rebuilt by sensors.
Turns body-camera footage into broadcast and training clips, and decides what is shown.
Tags every pass, tackle and shot by hand and with AI help, for data companies and clubs.

slides.notes:
STUDIO A · 2 MINUTES. One card per click. For each: "What skill does this need that the machine does not have?"

The tracking operator: semi-automated offside runs on up to 30 cameras per ground (Premier League, 2025). The sports scientist: FIFA allowed GPS and tracking systems in matches from 2015; sports science is now in every Premier League club, and academy and first-team sports scientist roles are advertised throughout the leagues. Data collectors: data companies employ people to tag event data, increasingly checking an AI’s first pass rather than tagging from scratch. That is how many analysts start.

slides.name: 25 · Framed picture
slides.notes: STUDIO B · 30 SECONDS. Engineer: the people who move and protect the data.

slides.name: 26 · Studio B · Engineer

params.text: Builds the pipelines that join tracking, event, GPS and medical data. Leeds United advertised one in 2025, up to £55,000.
Turns AI research into tools coaches use every day. Arsenal advertised one in 2026: Python, SQL, TypeScript, PyTorch.
Protects a club’s data, from medical records to transfer plans, from attack and leaks.
Makes sure fans’ and players’ personal data is used within the law.

slides.notes:
STUDIO B · 2 MINUTES. These are the jobs a computing or data student could apply for this year.

Leeds United’s data engineer/scientist advert (UK Sport jobs board, June 2025): building pipelines for data science across performance, medicine and recruitment, up to £55,000. Arsenal’s research engineer (Business Today, 24 July 2026): joining the data analytics team to work with the men’s first-team analysis department; to “turn advanced AI research into tools” the coaching staff use daily; asking for Python, SQL, JavaScript or TypeScript, and deep learning frameworks such as PyTorch, JAX or TensorFlow, plus an understanding of football. Brentford and Cardiff Metropolitan University funded a PhD studentship in Premier League performance data (2026).

Ask: "What does ‘an understanding of football’ add to a job advert for an engineer?"

slides.name: 27 · Framed picture
slides.notes: STUDIO C · 30 SECONDS. Model: the people who find the pattern and test the future.

slides.name: 28 · Studio C · Model

params.text: Builds models of space, passes and chances. Liverpool’s research team was led by physicists.
Brentford’s title for the man who made their set pieces a science, before Chelsea hired him in 2024.
Searches the world’s leagues in data before a scout ever travels.
Runs AI across recruitment, tactics and the business. Reading made one in 2026.

slides.notes:
STUDIO C · 2 MINUTES. William Spearman, Liverpool’s lead data scientist, has a physics PhD and worked at CERN; his best-known idea is pitch control, which parts of the pitch a team controls. He said: “I grew up being really bad at most team sports. I still am.” (The Mirror, September 2022, quoting Liverpoolfc.com.) You do not have to be good at football to work in it.

Bernardo Cueva: Brentford’s first-team tactical statistician, whose work was largely set pieces; he left for Chelsea to build a set-piece department (Brentford FC, May 2024). Stuart Fenton: Reading’s head of AI, working on recruitment, tactics and the business; Reading say AI complements the team and results are down to the coaches (BBC Sport, 6 March 2026).

slides.name: 29 · Framed picture
slides.notes: STUDIO D · 30 SECONDS. Design: the people who make the data seen and felt. For an art and design room, this is the studio to stay in longest.

slides.name: 30 · Studio D · Design

params.text: Designs the 3D offside replay, the live stats and the graphics a billion people watch.
Makes one pitch-side board show a different advert in every country, and still look real.
Fills a 360° roof screen, the lights and the sound, and designs the matchday as an experience.
Turns a model into a picture a coach reads in ten seconds at half-time.

slides.notes:
STUDIO D · 3 MINUTES. THE ART-STUDIO STUDIO. Every moment in part 01 ended at a picture: the 3D replay, the virtual board, the 360° screen, the referee’s POV. Each picture is a design brief.

The broadcast motion designer: the semi-automated offside decision visual is generated and sent to the big screen and broadcasters (Premier League, 2025). Somebody sets how it looks. The virtual ad producer: the overlay has to respond to light and be hidden by passing players to look real (BusinessCloud, 2018). The immersive venue designer: 3,700 m² of LED at the Bernabéu (Daktronics). Also on the atlas, the fan product designer: the club app, the AI chatbot and the second screen; Microsoft and the Premier League built an AI Companion for fans (Microsoft’s own figures, 2026). The data visualisation designer: a coach at half-time has minutes, not an hour.

Generative AI is now in this studio too: concept art for kits and campaigns, auto-cut highlights, translated commentary. Ask: "Which part of a designer’s job does generative AI take, and which part does it make more valuable?"

slides.name: 31 · Framed picture
slides.notes: STUDIO E · 30 SECONDS. Decide and care: the people who make the call and look after the humans the data is about.

slides.name: 32 · Studio E · Decide & care

params.text: Throw-ins, set pieces, kicking, the goalkeeper’s feet: a coach for each part data can measure.
Works on pressure, focus and confidence. Clubs now advertise these roles at first-team and academy level.
Trains how fast players scan and decide. Liverpool worked with neuro11 on penalties.
Asks the hard questions before a club uses a new AI, and after.

slides.notes:
STUDIO E · 2 MINUTES. The studio people forget, and the one AI makes more important, not less. The last step on the line is a person.

Specialist coaches: Grønnemark at Liverpool (2018); set-piece coaches across the Premier League as set pieces became 27.4% of goals (The Analyst, 2025–26). Performance psychologists: advertised at clubs such as Southampton and West Bromwich Albion’s academy (sport psychology job roundups). Neuro coaching: neuro11, a German neuroscience company, worked with Liverpool from 2021; Klopp credited them after the February 2022 League Cup final shootout (Ulrich Lichtenthaler, 2022). FC Copenhagen built a brain-training function led by a neuroscientist (Training Ground Guru). AI ethics lead: a role more common in big organisations than in clubs yet. Say so: it is an opening, not a crowded field.

slides.name: 33 · How new is this job?

params.text: The positions are arguable. That is the activity.

slides.notes:
PART 03 · 3 MINUTES. STAND ON THE LINE. One wall is "existed in 2010", the other "did not exist in 2015". Read each job; students move; then click to show ours.

The point: most jobs were not invented by AI; they were rebuilt by it. Only a few, like head of AI, are new titles. The data protection officer moves right because UK GDPR (2018) made the role a legal requirement for many organisations.

Ask: "Which of these will not exist in 2035?"

slides.name: 34 · Football × something else

params.text: Pitch control, ball flight, the space between players.
The replay, the stats, the screen in the roof.
Whose data is it, and who can sell it?

slides.notes:
PART 03 · 2 MINUTES. Every job on the atlas is football crossed with another discipline. Pairs say which cross they are, from their own course, and one job it leads to.

Take four answers. Write the crosses on the board: the brief will use them.

slides.name: 35 · Framed picture
slides.notes: PART 04 · 7 MINUTES. A studio crit. The rule of a crit: argue with the work, not the person.

slides.name: 36 · Statement · frame

params.text: If the offside line is a render, who is its author?
Hands up: the referee, the engineer, the designer · then reasons

slides.notes:
PART 04 · 2 MINUTES. Three-way vote. Then one reason from each.

The Premier League’s line: the VAR reviews and approves; the technology speeds it up. But the camera placement, the model, the kick-point suggestion and the 3D picture were all designed by someone. When a decision is disputed, fans argue with the picture.

Push: "If a designer’s replay makes a toenail offside look obvious, is that fair design or persuasion?"

slides.name: 37 · What AI brings and what people bring

params.text: What AI brings and what people bring
Tracks every joint, 100 times a second.
Decides what “level” should mean in the law.
Searches every league in the world.
Sees who will fit the dressing room.
Generates a thousand graphics a match.
Chooses the one that makes 60,000 people feel something.
Puts an arm round the one who missed.

slides.notes:
PART 04 · 2 MINUTES. Ulrich Lichtenthaler (2022) calls it integrated intelligence: Liverpool’s data paid off when it was combined with Klopp’s people skills. Read each AI cell, ask "and what do people bring?", then click.

The design row is the one to land for this room: generation is cheap; taste and judgement are not.

slides.name: 38 · Myth or fact?

params.text: It suggests the lines; the VAR approves the decision.
You need to be good at football to work in it
Liverpool’s lead data scientist says he is “really bad at most team sports”.
Arsenal advertised for a research engineer in 2026.
AI will replace the creative jobs first
The World Economic Forum lists creative thinking among the fastest-rising skills.

slides.notes:
PART 04 · 2 MINUTES. Thumbs up for fact, down for myth, then click.

Row 4 is the honest one: nobody knows. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 lists creative thinking, with AI and big data, among the skills employers expect to grow most by 2030; it also expects graphic designers to be among the roles that decline. Both are in the same report. Ask: "How can both be true?" (The task is automated; the judgement is not.)

slides.name: 39 · Statement · frame

params.text: A player’s body is tracked every day for years. Who owns that data when they leave?

slides.notes:
PART 04 · 1 MINUTE. The question under every studio. The player, the club, the data company, the next club? Under UK data protection law the player can ask what is held about them; health data is special category data with extra protection. In 2021 Project Red Card, a group of players backed by former manager Russell Slade, threatened legal action over data companies using players’ performance data without consent.

That is a job too: Studio B’s data protection officer, Studio E’s ethics lead.

slides.name: 40 · Framed picture
slides.notes: PART 05 · 11 MINUTES. The output of the session. Teams of three, mixing courses if you can.

slides.name: 41 · Design a football job for 2035

params.text: Find a part of football nobody measures, designs or looks after yet. Invent the job that does it, put it on the line, and make its poster.
The brief · teams of three · 12 minutes

slides.notes:
PART 05 · 1 MINUTE TO SET. Start points from the session: the parts nobody has measured (from the numbers slide), the crosses (football × your discipline), and the catches from the crit.

The constraint that makes it good: the job must name its catch. A job with no catch is an advert.

slides.name: 42 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
PART 05 · 8 MINUTES TO MAKE. Leave this up while they work. A3 and markers, or one slide per team. Walk the room and push on field 4: if AI could do the whole job, it is not a job.

Examples to unstick a team (do not show unless stuck): crowd-noise designer, who tunes the sound of a stadium; academy data guardian, who decides what a 12-year-old’s tracking data can be used for; multilingual AI commentary editor; women’s game data scout, where data is scarcer; stadium digital-twin operator, who runs crowd simulations before matchday (Athletic Club’s San Mamés has been modelled this way, BCAM, 2025).

slides.name: 43 · Crit rules

params.text: Sixty seconds: the gap, the job, the human part.
The room asks one question, about the catch.
One team builds on it: what would make this job better?

slides.notes:
PART 05 · 2 MINUTES FOR THREE OR FOUR TEAMS. Pin the posters up on the wall beside the atlas, at the step on the line each job claims. The wall is the session’s output; photograph it.

If time is short, do a gallery walk: everyone puts a dot on the job they would apply for.

slides.name: 44 · Statement · frame

params.text: Football’s next great signing might be a designer.

slides.notes:
CLOSE. Back to the throw-in coach: a job that looked weird in 2018 because nobody had measured throw-ins. The jobs on the wall look weird today for the same reason.

Follow-up: Jobs In Football and Training Ground Guru list club roles; the World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 is free to read.
